name: Bilal Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior buyer at Summit Beverage and Snack Distribution. We supply about 500 convenience stores, petrol stations and vending operators with soft drinks, water, crisps and sweets. I start at 6:30 looking at what sold over the weekend, then I plan the promotions with the big brands, who all want shelf space. By afternoon I'm negotiating next quarter's volumes and arguing about who pays for a damaged pallet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm of it, and the fact that it's a plain, honest business. People drink and snack in good times and bad. I like the brand reps, who've become old friends. What wears me out is the pressure on margins and the endless promotions, and the new ordering assistant that the company wants us to trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, we can stop worrying and get on. At work I'd say let's use what helps and not make a fuss. At church I'd say we've survived worse, and we'll look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Soft drinks and crisps don't change because of a chatbot. People still get thirsty at four o'clock, and I still have to guess how thirsty. But it doesn't help my money. I'm 58, on lower pay than the big-city buyers, and we've got under a month saved after helping Hannah and Jonah through their training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job as I do, with the assistant for routine reorders, which I already use now and then. I'd ask my boss about a raise and take on the seasonal planning for the whole region, so I'm worth more. Sofia and I would trim a bit. And I'd keep the Saturday morning job helping a friend run a stall at the farmers' market, which brings in a bit extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, a bit tired. It's not frightening. But I'd like to retire without counting every coin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping your children. How does that affect your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wife Sofia cleans at the school and sings in the choir, and her wage is small but steady. We help Jonah with his trade-school fees and Hannah with her rent as she trains as a care assistant. That went into the savings. We've still got a mortgage with seven years to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got worse at Summit anyway, what would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the supermarkets, the energy bills and the rules that make small firms like ours do more paperwork. It wouldn't be the machines. It would be the cost of doing business with ten people when you're up against chains with a thousand.

say: I'd say good, we can stop worrying and **get on**.
At church I'd say we've survived worse and will **look after each other**.
think: Soft drinks don't change because of a chatbot, but my **money** is thin.
I'm on lower pay and have under a month saved after the **children's training**.
do: Use the assistant for **routine reorders** and take on seasonal planning for the region.
Keep the Saturday **market stall** job for extra cash.
feel: **Settled, a bit tired**; I'd like to retire without counting every coin.
S0.quote: Soft drinks and crisps don't change because of a chatbot. People still get thirsty at four o'clock, and I still have to guess how thirsty.
fieldNote: A **sturdy, ordinary** job feels safe from AI, but the money, with two children in training, still weighs.
Blames supermarkets, energy costs and paperwork rules, a free-market view of small firms squeezed.

steps.text: Keep planning promotions and reorders for the 500 shops
Keep the Saturday market stall job for extra cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's use the tools when they're proven and keep our feet on the ground. At work I'd say we shouldn't rush. At church I'd say we should help the young learn trades that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The assistant has been wrong about the summer promotions twice, and I fixed both. The day it stops being wrong is the day they stop needing me. I think about a third of the buying job goes to it in three years, and the firm will trim the team from six to four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the ordering assistant properly, so I'm the one who knows where it fails. I'd ask for a team-lead role. I'd also put my name down for weekend driving shifts at a local courier, which I could do for about 300 a month. And I'd save every spare coin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not frozen. I've been through changes at work before, and I know how to push through. But this one has a shape I haven't seen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Hannah and Jonah?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get a trade that needs a person. Hannah's care work is safer for years. Jonah's electrical course is good, but he should learn estimating and ordering too. I'd tell them both to keep a bit of money aside, and to stay close to the church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which colleague worries you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Sven, the junior buyer, who's quick but green. I'd tell him to learn the tools and the people side, which are the only two things that will keep him. I'd be honest that the firm's plan isn't clear, and I wouldn't pretend.

say: I'd say use the tools **when proven** and keep our feet on the ground.
At church I'd say we should help the young learn **trades**.
think: The assistant was wrong about summer promotions twice, and the day it stops is the day I'm **not needed**.
The firm will trim the team from **six to four**.
do: Learn the **ordering assistant** properly so I know where it fails.
Take weekend **courier** shifts for about 300 a month.
feel: **Anxious but not frozen**; this change has a shape I haven't seen.
S1.quote: The assistant has been wrong about the summer promotions twice, and I fixed both. The day it stops being wrong is the day they stop needing me.
fieldNote: Steady and practical: he learns the tool to **know where it fails**, and adds a second income.
Gives his children trade advice, linking family and work.

steps.text: Learn the ordering assistant well enough to catch its failures
Ask for a team-lead role before the team shrinks
Take weekend courier shifts for about 300 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and that someone should slow it down, though I know nobody will. At work I'd say let's hold steady and see what our bosses do. At church I'd say let's stay close to each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too fast for a man who still pays a mortgage. I think my desk job goes, the buying and planning, because that's what the card says goes first. The vans and the warehouse last until the robots, about three years later. My money doesn't last that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold on to the job, work any extra shift, and ask the church to help us carry what we can't. I'd go to my boss about moving to the delivery side. I'd also ask about driving for the courier full-time, since that's not likely to be automated until around 2031. And we'd cut everything except food and the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's a hard knot in my chest. I'd pray more and sleep less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a move to delivery work mean for your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At about 58 with a mortgage, I'd maybe get four months of work in whatever comes up. A full-time delivery job pays less than I earn now. It'd be a pay cut of about a third. But it's a wage, and Sofia's school work adds to it. We'd manage, barely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly the people who push it so hard, the big companies and the investors who want a quick return. Politicians too, for not preparing us. I wouldn't blame Summit. The owners are decent people and they'd be caught in the same storm.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and someone should slow it down.
At work I'd say let's **hold steady** and see what the bosses do.
think: My desk job goes **first**, and the vans and warehouse last about three years longer.
My money doesn't last that long, with a **mortgage** still running.
do: Work every extra **shift** and ask the church for help.
Ask my boss about moving to **delivery** work.
Cut everything except food and the **mortgage**.
feel: **Alarmed**; a hard knot in my chest, more prayer and less sleep.
S2.quote: I'd hold on to the job, work any extra shift, and ask the church to help us carry what we can't.
fieldNote: Plans a **move to hands-on work**, delivery, exactly where the timeline gives him three more years.
Accepts a third less pay, and blames investors and politicians rather than his employer.

steps.text: Ask to move to the delivery side or drive for the courier
Cut everything except food and the mortgage
Ask the church community to help carry what we can't

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a decent chance and we shouldn't waste it. At work I'd say learn the tools now and keep your own judgement. At church I'd say we should help families with training for the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the buying desk is shaky by year three or four, and I'd be 63. Give me five years and I'll have the mortgage down and a few weekend jobs lined up, so I'm never at the mercy of one employer. I'd hope to be out before the worst of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd get the ordering assistant working for me, and take on the supplier relationships it can't. I'd keep the stall job and the courier shifts, and pay down the mortgage by 300 a month. I'd also train Sven, so my knowledge doesn't leave when I do. And I'd talk to Summit about part-time work until 65.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mix of steady and worried. I don't panic in five years. I just keep my sleeves rolled up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your employer for, if you could?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my boss and ask what the plan is for the buying team. If they're willing, I'd ask to go to four days a week at 62. And I'd ask the same of Sofia. A bit less income, but we'd have more time together, and the house paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where is the plan weakest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly about the 59 to 62 years. Because the thin savings will have been used on the mortgage, and I'd be stuck with the pension at 65. If the firm lets me go at 61, I'd have two or three years of bridging with weekend work. It's possible, but tight.

say: I'd say five years gives us a **decent chance** and we shouldn't waste it.
I'd tell colleagues to learn the tools and keep their own **judgement**.
think: The buying desk is **shaky** by year three or four, when I'm 63.
I'd hope to be out **before the worst** of it.

Pay down the mortgage by **300 a month**.
Train **Sven** and ask Summit about part-time work until 65.
feel: **Steady but worried**; I'd keep my sleeves rolled up.
S3.quote: Give me five years and I'll have the mortgage down and a few weekend jobs lined up, so I'm never at the mercy of one employer.
fieldNote: His plan stacks **small incomes**, the stall and courier shifts, so no single employer decides his fate.
Names the weak years honestly: bridging from 61 to 65 on weekend work.

steps.text: Get the ordering assistant working for me within a year
Keep the stall job and weekend courier shifts
Pay down the mortgage by 300 a month
Ask Summit about part-time work from 62 to 65

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's a decent runway, and we should use it. At work I'd say keep learning. At church I'd say let's make sure the young have trades and a bit of land or savings behind them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years I'll be retired and my youngest son Jonah will be in the thick of it, and that's the part that keeps me up. For me it's mostly fine. I'd work until 65, then maybe do a few part-time days if my back lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work, and take the assistant as it improves. I'd pay down the mortgage by 250 a month and put a bit into a pension top-up. I'd keep the market stall going. And I'd help Jonah with his electrical course and teach him the buying side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. I'd say I'm uneasy more than anxious. It's the worry for the children, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jonah about his own work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him that the thinking part of his trade, the estimating and ordering, is what a machine takes first. The hands-on part has three more years. I'd tell him to learn to run a small business, to be the one who decides and signs. It's the best thing I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a decent retirement look like for you and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the mortgage done and some savings, and we'd sit with a pension that covers the basics. Sofia would stay at the school as long as she liked. Maybe we'd have a small cabin. It's not much, but it'd be ours. And the choir on Sundays.

say: I'd say good, it's a decent **runway**, so use it.
At church I'd say make sure the young have **trades** and savings behind them.
think: In ten years I'll be retired, but **Jonah** will be in the thick of it.
For me it's mostly fine; the worry is for the **children**.
do: Work till **65** and take the assistant as it improves.
Pay down the mortgage by **250 a month** and add a small pension top-up.
Teach **Jonah** the buying and estimating side.
feel: **Uneasy** more than anxious; the worry is for the children, not for me.
S4.quote: In ten years I'll be retired and my youngest son Jonah will be in the thick of it, and that's the part that keeps me up.
fieldNote: The long runway makes him **safe personally**; his concern turns to his youngest son's trade.
Wants a simple retirement: mortgage paid, small pension, choir on Sundays.

steps.text: Pay down the mortgage by 250 a month and add a pension top-up
Teach Jonah the estimating and ordering side of his trade
Work until 65 and keep the market stall going

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. A mortgage with years left and nothing saved, and no time to do anything. What would help is a fair notice period, a pension I can count on, and the chance to move to work that needs a person. And my church, which is already helping.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm no good at asking for help. I've never asked anybody for a handout and I'm not starting now, but I'd take a fair deal on notice and a decent pension. And I'd like someone to remember that those of us who kept things running aren't asking for much.

headlineQuote: I've never asked anybody for a handout and I'm not starting now, but I'd take a fair deal on notice and a decent pension.
portrait: Bilal Baker, 58, is the **senior buyer** at a beverage and snack distributor serving about 500 stores and vending operators.
He uses the company's ordering assistant **now and then**, and has under a month saved after two children's training.
He's traditional and free-market, leans on **church and family**, and blames big firms and politicians, not his bosses.
His mood rises from uneasy to **alarmed** if AGI arrives in two years.
He'd stack **small incomes**, such as a market stall and courier shifts, and move toward hands-on work.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, with a mortgage still running and nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **notice period**, a pension he can count on, and a chance to move into work that needs a person.
